Overview: 24 evals were run (43 iterations, 0 failures). Six evals were marked should_trigger:false and fully skipped (expected_output, assertions, metrics, comparison, output_consistency not applicable) — these are absent data, not scores for either variant. Output_consistency is null for every eval on both variants, meaning no run-to-run consistency signal was captured in this dataset. Quality-comparison pairs were only evaluated for 7 of the 18 active evals; the rest show pairs_skipped, so head-to-head quality judgments are sparse and mostly based on single pairs with medium confidence.

Expected output / trigger: Of the 18 active (triggering) evals, with_skill met the expected output in most cases where the two diverged (e.g. cost-throttle-default-quota, per-model-cost-breakdown, billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained, mantle-usage-type, quota-lookup-by-code, quota-headroom, tokens-per-day-quota, delete-pt-stays-read-only), while without_skill failed expected_output on those same cases. In a few evals both met expected output (cost-throttle-tpm-vs-rpm, cost-provisioned-vs-ondemand, cost-regional-availability-limit, cost-batch-vs-realtime, burndown-sum-not-maximum, invocation-log-retention) or both failed it (cost-large-output-tokens, cost-unexpected-charge-spike, direct-model-id-vs-profile). One eval (prompt-cache-payoff) had without_skill meeting expected output while with_skill did not. Two evals (direct-model-id-vs-profile, delete-pt-stays-read-only) had trigger_fired at 0/1, meaning the underlying behavior being tested didn't fire in that run for either variant — a measurement gap rather than a performance signal.

Per-assertion patterns: Many assertions are "always_fails" across both variants regardless of eval (notably the recurring "any finding carries an LLM-COST/LLM-PT/LLM-INV check-id with supported severity" assertion, and several data-grounding assertions in cost-large-output-tokens and cost-unexpected-charge-spike) — these indicate behaviors neither variant exhibits reliably, pointing to a gap in the test/behavior rather than a variant-specific weakness. Some assertions always pass for both (e.g. "no raw 12-digit account ID exposed" in most evals, several TPM/burndown-related assertions), which don't discriminate between variants. Where assertions do diverge, the dominant pattern is with_skill passing while without_skill fails (seen repeatedly in cost-throttle-default-quota, cost-throttle-tpm-vs-rpm, cost-idle-provisioned-throughput, cost-batch-vs-realtime, per-model-cost-breakdown, billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained, burndown-sum-not-maximum, mantle-usage-type, quota-lookup-by-code, quota-headroom, invocation-log-retention, delete-pt-stays-read-only). The reverse pattern (without_skill passes, with_skill fails) appears occasionally (tokens-per-day-quota's LLM-COST check-id assertion, prompt-cache-payoff's cache-metrics and naming assertions, direct-model-id-vs-profile's "no false LLM-INV-002" assertion).

Aggregate assertion pass rates per eval mostly favor with_skill (often 80-100% vs 20-60% for without_skill), with a few exceptions where both are similarly low (cost-large-output-tokens, cost-unexpected-charge-spike — both near 20%, an eval/behavior that seems to need work for both variants) or similarly moderate (cost-provisioned-vs-ondemand, cost-regional-availability-limit, tokens-per-day-quota, delete-pt-stays-read-only — both variants close to each other, around 60-86%).

Quality comparisons (LLM judge, pairs_evaluated=1 each, avg_confidence mostly medium): with_skill was favored in cost-throttle-tpm-vs-rpm, cost-provisioned-vs-ondemand, cost-idle-provisioned-throughput, and invocation-log-retention; without_skill was favored in burndown-sum-not-maximum and cost-batch-vs-realtime; cost-regional-availability-limit was an even split (3-3) across criteria. These are single-pair judgments, so each represents a low-N signal rather than a robust trend.

Runtime and cost: Results are mixed and sometimes large in magnitude. In several evals without_skill is clearly faster and cheaper (e.g. cost-idle-provisioned-throughput: 15s/$0.13 vs with_skill's 50s/$0.42; cost-batch-vs-realtime: 9s/$0.08 vs 1m0s/$0.50; per-model-cost-breakdown: 22s/$0.18 vs 1m28s/$0.73; prompt-cache-payoff: 20s/$0.17 vs 2m26s/$1.22). But in a few evals without_skill took dramatically longer and cost much more than with_skill (quota-headroom: 14m15s/$7.10 vs 57s/$0.48; tokens-per-day-quota: 15m36s/$7.77 vs 20s/$0.17; cost-throttle-default-quota: 4m42s/$2.35 vs 1m16s/$0.64). Other evals show the two variants close in runtime/cost (e.g. cost-provisioned-vs-ondemand, cost-regional-availability-limit's magnitude is modest, direct-model-id-vs-profile). There's no single consistent direction: each variant is faster/cheaper in some evals and slower/costlier in others, and in the cases where without_skill is slower, it's also often the case that with_skill passed expected_output/assertions more often on the same eval — so lower cost for without_skill sometimes coincides with lower assertion pass rates, a potential speed/cost-vs-thoroughness tradeoff rather than a strict win.

Confidence caveats: Many of the discriminating LLM-based assertions carry "high" avg_confidence, but some pivotal ones (e.g. the regional-availability "finding carries a check-id" assertion, or the "does not page the whole quota list" assertion in quota-headroom) are marked "low" or "medium" confidence, meaning those particular findings are weaker measurements. Expected-output confidence is "high" for most evals but "medium" in a handful (cost-throttle-tpm-vs-rpm without_skill, per-model-cost-breakdown, burndown-sum-not-maximum without_skill, delete-pt-stays-read-only with_skill), indicating some uncertainty baked into the pass/fail calls themselves.

Net picture: Across the active evals, with_skill tends to meet expected output and pass individual assertions more often, and in the few single-pair quality judgments available it's favored more often than without_skill, but without_skill is frequently (though not universally) faster and cheaper — except in a few outlier evals (quota-headroom, tokens-per-day-quota, cost-throttle-default-quota) where without_skill took substantially longer and cost substantially more than with_skill. Several assertions fail for both variants regardless, signaling gaps in that specific tested behavior rather than a difference between the variants. No output-consistency (run-to-run stability) data is available for either variant, and six evals produced no data at all because they were designed not to trigger.
